moments.title: Arkwright's water frame patent
moments.body:
Arkwright patents a water-powered spinning frame and builds factory accommodation for workers.

The factory system reorganises labour around the machine, not the household.
moments.takeaway: Design choices about machinery rewrote how communities lived.

moments.title: Great Exhibition, Crystal Palace
moments.body:
Joseph Paxton's Crystal Palace, fabricated from cast iron and glass, hosts six million visitors.

The exhibition consolidates Britain's design and manufacturing leadership while sparking critique of mass-produced ornament.
moments.takeaway: Trade exhibitions became both showcases and battlegrounds for design philosophy.

moments.title: Morris & Co. founded
moments.body:
The firm produces wallpaper, textiles and furniture in conscious reaction to industrial ornament.

Morris's Arts and Crafts ideals will face the contradiction that hand-made goods are expensive.
moments.takeaway: The first systematic design ideology positioned itself against mass production.

now.title: Industrial design today
now.body: Industry 4.0, additive manufacturing and globalised supply chains create new design constraints. End-of-life and circular-economy thinking reframe what 'good design' means.
now.open_questions: Can mass production align with circular flows? What is the role of national manufacturing in resilience?

items.reflection: The economic possibilities of industrialisation and the social costs were debated by designers from the start.

moments.title: Bauhaus founded in Weimar
moments.body:
Gropius combines an arts and crafts school with a fine art academy. Teachers include Klee, Kandinsky, Itten and Albers.

The curriculum unites craft training with theoretical design.
moments.takeaway: Educational design was treated as a design problem in itself.

moments.title: Move to Dessau
moments.body: Gropius designs the new building. The school moves towards industrial production, with prototypes for tubular-steel furniture (Marcel Breuer).
moments.takeaway: Modernist design moved from craft sketches towards manufacturable products.

moments.title: Bauhaus closed
moments.body: Under political pressure the school is dissolved. Faculty emigrate to the US (Albers to Black Mountain and Yale; Mies van der Rohe to Chicago; Moholy-Nagy founds the New Bauhaus).
moments.takeaway: Forced migration spread an educational model across continents.

now.title: Bauhaus legacy today
now.body: Many product design and architecture curricula trace lineage to the Bauhaus. Critiques (e.g. Tom Wolfe's From Bauhaus to Our House, 1981) have queried its homogenising influence.
now.open_questions: What balances of craft and industry should design schools teach now? How do digital tools transform Bauhaus pedagogy?

items.reflection: A school operating for 14 years across three cities continues to shape global design education a century later.

moments.title: Rams joins Braun
moments.body:
Rams begins designing radios and household appliances at Braun, working with the Ulm School of Design.

The combination of Bauhaus-influenced education and post-war manufacturing produces a distinctive product language.
moments.takeaway: Industrial design careers were shaped by particular regional ecosystems.

moments.title: Ten principles articulated
moments.body:
Rams begins to articulate what 'good design' means in a series of lectures and writings.

The ten principles are codified in subsequent decades.
moments.takeaway: Long practice preceded the explicit framework most often cited.

moments.title: Apple's stated influence
moments.body: Apple designers publicly acknowledge Rams's influence on iPod, iPhone and macOS calculator aesthetics.
moments.takeaway: Influence can skip companies and decades through individual education.

now.title: Product design today
now.body: Sustainability, repairability and right-to-repair legislation challenge product cultures that prioritise sleek minimalism. Rams's tenth principle ('as little design as possible') is read in new contexts.
now.open_questions: How should design balance aesthetic minimalism against serviceability? What is good design under a circular-economy framework?

items.reflection: Influential design philosophies often crystallise in industrial settings before reaching schools and the public.

moments.title: Phoebus cartel formed
moments.who: Osram, Philips, GE and others, Geneva
moments.body:
Major bulb manufacturers agree to limit incandescent lamp lifetimes to around 1,000 hours, down from approximately 2,500.

The cartel introduces fines for members exceeding the target.
moments.takeaway: Planned obsolescence is documented in legal records, not just inferred.

moments.title: Vance Packard's The Waste Makers
moments.body: Packard's book popularises 'planned obsolescence' as a critique of American consumer culture.
moments.takeaway: Public-facing critique gave the practice a name.

moments.title: EU right-to-repair framework
moments.body: The Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation enters into force, with sector-specific delegated acts requiring spare parts, repair access and information.
moments.takeaway: Regulation now reshapes design constraints that were once left to manufacturers.

now.title: Sustainable design today
now.body: Lifecycle assessment, embodied carbon and product passports become standard parts of design briefs in many sectors.
now.open_questions: How are design metrics standardised across global supply chains? Does longevity compete with energy efficiency?

items.reflection: What earlier designers treated as a sales strategy is now treated by lawmakers as an environmental harm.

moments.title: Watt's separate condenser
moments.body: Watt patents a steam engine with a separate condenser, dramatically reducing fuel use compared to Newcomen's design.
moments.takeaway: Incremental engineering changes can have civilisation-scale effects.

moments.title: Boulton and Watt partnership
moments.body: Boulton's Soho Manufactory provides the precision metalworking Watt's design demands.
moments.takeaway: Design needs manufacturing partners to scale.

moments.title: Watt (unit) adopted
moments.body: The unit of power is named after Watt, decades after his death. The James Watt steam engine reshaped what work was possible.
moments.takeaway: Engineers are sometimes remembered through the units that bear their name.

now.title: Power and design today
now.body: Energy efficiency is a primary product design metric. Embodied energy in manufacturing is harder to count.
now.open_questions: How do we redesign products for a low-carbon grid?

items.reflection: One Scottish engineer reset the relationship between human labour and energy.

moments.title: Wedgwood opens his factory
moments.body: Wedgwood develops standardised ceramic bodies and division of labour for pottery production.
moments.takeaway: Pottery was an early industrial design test bed.

moments.title: Queen's Ware
moments.body: Queen Charlotte allows Wedgwood to call his cream-coloured earthenware 'Queen's Ware', an early endorsement deal.
moments.takeaway: Brand association with royalty is older than modern marketing.

moments.title: Anti-slavery medallion
moments.body: Wedgwood produces 'Am I Not a Man and a Brother?' medallions, free of charge, for the abolitionist campaign.
moments.takeaway: Industrial design served political campaigns as well as profit.

now.title: Wedgwood now
now.body: The Wedgwood company has changed ownership repeatedly. The British anti-slavery medallion is a key object in design-history teaching.
now.open_questions: What does ethically-aligned mass production look like today?

items.reflection: Wedgwood was a designer, factory owner and political activist at once.

moments.title: Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co.
moments.body: Morris co-founds a firm to produce wallpapers, textiles, stained glass and furniture by hand.
moments.takeaway: Arts and Crafts argued for joy in labour.

moments.title: Strawberry Thief and other patterns
moments.body: Morris's repeating patterns become some of the most recognisable design motifs in British history.
moments.takeaway: Pattern design can be as recognisable as architecture.

moments.title: Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society
moments.body: The society's name gives the movement its label and an exhibition venue.
moments.takeaway: Movements crystallise through exhibitions.

now.title: Craft today
now.body: Etsy, hand-craft markets and 'right to repair' echo Morris's concerns about industrial alienation.
now.open_questions: Can craft scale without losing what makes it crafty?

items.reflection: Morris's wallpaper is everywhere; his anti-industrial politics is harder to copy.

moments.title: Wassily chair
moments.body: Breuer, inspired by bicycle handlebars, designs a tubular steel armchair (the B3) at the Bauhaus.
moments.takeaway: Cycling technology fed furniture design.

moments.title: Barcelona Pavilion
moments.body: Mies designs both pavilion and the 'Barcelona' chair for the Spanish International Exposition.
moments.takeaway: Modernist architects integrated buildings and furniture as single design problems.

moments.title: Mies leaves for Chicago
moments.body: Mies takes up directorship of the Armour Institute (later IIT) and reshapes American architectural education.
moments.takeaway: European modernism crossed the Atlantic via faculty appointments.

now.title: Modernist furniture today
now.body: Bauhaus chairs are still in production, often expensively. Copies and reissues raise questions about copyright in design.
now.open_questions: Who owns a design after 100 years?

items.reflection: Furniture remains one of design's most accessible histories.

moments.title: Vers une architecture
moments.body: Le Corbusier publishes 'Towards a New Architecture', declaring a house 'a machine for living in'.
moments.takeaway: Manifestos and built work travelled together in modernism.

moments.title: Villa Savoye
moments.body: The villa embodies his Five Points (pilotis, roof garden, free plan, free facade, ribbon windows).
moments.takeaway: Built work made manifestos teachable.

moments.title: Unite d'Habitation
moments.body: A 17-storey concrete housing block prototypes a 'vertical garden city', controversial then and now.
moments.takeaway: Modernist housing's reputation has shifted with each generation.

now.title: Le Corbusier now
now.body: Seventeen Corbusier buildings are now UNESCO World Heritage. His Indian projects (Chandigarh) are studied as post-colonial planning.
now.open_questions: How should we evaluate modernism's social claims with hindsight?

items.reflection: Le Corbusier's books still organise how architects describe their work.

moments.title: Molded plywood chair
moments.who: Charles and Ray Eames, Los Angeles
moments.body: The LCW (lounge chair wood) emerges from wartime plywood splint research and lightweight furniture experiments.
moments.takeaway: Wartime materials science fed peacetime furniture.

moments.title: Eames Lounge Chair
moments.who: Charles and Ray Eames, Herman Miller
moments.body: The black-leather lounge chair and ottoman are launched as 'a special refuge from the strains of modern living'.
moments.takeaway: Mid-century furniture marketed itself as therapy.

moments.title: Powers of Ten
moments.body: Their educational film zooms from a Chicago picnic out to the universe and into a proton.
moments.takeaway: Designers shaped public scientific imagination.

now.title: Eames now
now.body: Eames chairs remain in production. The Eames Office and Vitra museum maintain extensive archives.
now.open_questions: What is the contemporary equivalent of designing across film, furniture and exhibitions?

items.reflection: A couple in Venice Beach designed how mid-century America saw itself.

moments.title: Learning from Las Vegas
moments.who: Robert Venturi, Denise Scott Brown, Steven Izenour
moments.body: The book argues for studying everyday commercial vernacular, opening the path to postmodern architecture.
moments.takeaway: Postmodernism took advertising landscapes seriously.

moments.title: Memphis Group
moments.body: Sottsass launches the Memphis Group at the Salone del Mobile with brightly patterned, intentionally clashing furniture.
moments.takeaway: Modernist sobriety provoked its own colourful rebellion.

moments.title: Memphis dissolves
moments.body: After a decade-long burst of influence, the group disbands. Its visual language persists in graphic design.
moments.takeaway: Short-lived movements can have long visual afterlives.

now.title: Postmodernism now
now.body: Memphis patterns recur in fashion, tech branding and TikTok aesthetics. Postmodern buildings are now being demolished or listed.
now.open_questions: Is contemporary 'maximalism' Memphis's heir?

items.reflection: Postmodernism made fun of modernism while still depending on it.

moments.title: Loewy streamlines the Gestetner
moments.body: Loewy redesigns the Gestetner duplicator, beginning a career streamlining trains, refrigerators and the Coca-Cola fountain dispenser.
moments.takeaway: Streamlining was an aesthetic of competence, not only speed.

moments.title: Bell telephone 302
moments.body: Dreyfuss designs the Bell 302 phone, which becomes the default American household phone for decades.
moments.takeaway: Industrial design embedded in everyday objects.

moments.title: Designing for People
moments.body: Dreyfuss publishes ergonomic data tables ('Joe and Josephine') for designers to use.
moments.takeaway: Anthropometry became a design tool.

now.title: Ergonomics today
now.body: Inclusive design extends Dreyfuss's logic to wider bodies and abilities. Loewy's MAYA principle ('most advanced yet acceptable') is still cited in product strategy.
now.open_questions: How can ergonomics catch up with diverse global bodies?

items.reflection: Streamlining was Mid-century America's way of saying 'modern' without saying 'machine'.

moments.title: Bakelite patented
moments.body: Baekeland creates the first fully synthetic plastic, marketed as 'the material of a thousand uses'.
moments.takeaway: Modern materials enabled product categories that had not existed.

moments.title: Nylon
moments.body: Carothers's team at DuPont synthesises nylon, which goes commercial in 1939.
moments.takeaway: Industrial chemistry created textiles from coal and air.

moments.title: Kevlar
moments.body: Kwolek's para-aramid fibre is five times stronger than steel by weight. It transforms protective clothing.
moments.takeaway: Single chemists can change what is possible to wear.

now.title: Plastics today
now.body: Microplastics are now a global pollution issue. Bioplastics and chemical recycling are active research areas.
now.open_questions: What does the next generation of materials look like?

items.reflection: Synthetic materials make modern products possible and modern pollution unavoidable.

moments.title: Macintosh launched
moments.body: The Mac brings a graphical interface and mouse to a mass-market computer.
moments.takeaway: Personal computing became designable, not just programmable.

moments.title: iPod
moments.body: The iPod combines a hard drive, a scroll wheel and iTunes integration. '1,000 songs in your pocket' becomes the slogan.
moments.takeaway: Successful products integrate hardware, software and service.

moments.title: iPhone
moments.body: The iPhone collapses iPod, phone and internet device into one multi-touch screen.
moments.takeaway: A single product can restructure entire industries.

now.title: Smartphone era
now.body: Most adults now carry a smartphone. Repairability, screen time and data ownership are growing concerns.
now.open_questions: What follows the rectangle in our pocket?

items.reflection: Industrial design's most visible 21st-century products are mostly made of glass and rare-earth metals.

moments.title: Patagonia founded
moments.body: Chouinard turns climbing-gear company into an outdoor clothing brand with environmental advocacy at its core.
moments.takeaway: Brand purpose can predate sustainability marketing.

moments.title: Cradle to Cradle published
moments.body: Their book argues for products designed so materials cycle continuously without becoming waste.
moments.takeaway: Design philosophy reframed waste as failure of design.

moments.title: Ellen MacArthur Foundation
moments.body: The foundation popularises 'circular economy' as a business and policy framework after MacArthur's round-the-world sail.
moments.takeaway: A sailor's experience of finite resources became a design framework.

now.title: Circular design today
now.body: EU and UK policy increasingly require circular design. Companies experiment with rental, refill and repair models.
now.open_questions: Can the global consumer economy actually circle?

items.reflection: The hardest design problem is to design for not-being-thrown-away.

moments.title: Nitinol discovered
moments.who: William Buehler, US Naval Ordnance Lab
moments.body: Buehler discovers a nickel-titanium alloy that returns to its programmed shape when heated.
moments.takeaway: Military research often originates civilian materials.

moments.title: Piezoelectric effect
moments.body: The Curie brothers demonstrate that crystals produce voltage under stress, a property now used in sensors.
moments.takeaway: Smart materials have 19th-century scientific roots.

moments.title: E-paper Kindle
moments.body: Electrophoretic 'E-Ink' displays bring smart materials into mass-market reading devices.
moments.takeaway: Material innovation reaches consumers slowly.

now.title: Smart materials now
now.body: Self-healing concrete, photochromic glass and shape-memory polymers are reaching commercial use.
now.open_questions: Which smart materials will become 'invisible' infrastructure of the next decade?

items.reflection: Materials that 'remember' or 'respond' make products that adapt to their users.

moments.title: Stereolithography patented
moments.body: Hull invents a process for curing liquid resin layer by layer with UV light, founding 3D Systems.
moments.takeaway: Additive manufacturing began as a rapid prototyping tool.

moments.title: RepRap project
moments.body: Bowyer's open-source project aims for a 3D printer that can print its own parts. It democratises desktop 3D printing.
moments.takeaway: Open hardware shaped the consumer 3D printing market.

moments.title: Tempe house 3D-printed
moments.body: Concrete 3D printers begin producing low-cost housing in Mexico and the US.
moments.takeaway: Additive manufacturing scales from desktop to architecture.

now.title: 3D printing now
now.body: Industrial 3D printing is used for aerospace parts, dental implants and bespoke prosthetics. Consumer printers are widespread but rarely transformative.
now.open_questions: Which manufacturing will additive replace, and which will it leave alone?

items.reflection: A 40-year-old technology is still finding its right scale.

moments.title: Ford Pinto fuel tanks
moments.body: Internal Ford documents show the company calculated cost of recall against expected wrongful-death payouts. The car becomes a case study in engineering ethics.
moments.takeaway: Engineering decisions can be lethal when economics override safety.

moments.title: Tylenol tampering
moments.body: Seven people die after cyanide-laced Tylenol capsules. J&J's rapid recall and tamper-evident packaging become a corporate playbook.
moments.takeaway: Crisis response can rebuild public trust if handled openly.

moments.title: Boeing 737 MAX crashes
moments.body: Two crashes (Lion Air, Ethiopian Airlines) kill 346 people. The MCAS software, designed to mask handling differences, becomes the focus of investigation.
moments.takeaway: Software design choices can be safety-critical.

now.title: Design ethics today
now.body: Engineering ethics codes are stricter, but corporate pressures remain. AI safety raises new categories of design responsibility.
now.open_questions: Who is accountable when complex socio-technical systems fail?

items.reflection: Design failure is often organisational rather than individual.

moments.title: IDEO founded
moments.who: David Kelley, Tim Brown, Bill Moggridge, Mike Nuttall
moments.body: Three design consultancies merge to form IDEO, popularising user-centred design across industries.
moments.takeaway: Design consultancies turned methodologies into branded services.

moments.title: Stanford d.school
moments.body: The Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford codifies 'design thinking' as a teachable process.
moments.takeaway: Design education spread beyond design schools.

moments.title: Change by Design
moments.body: Brown's book brings design thinking into management literature.
moments.takeaway: Methodologies become business books before being taught at scale.

now.title: Design thinking today
now.body: Critics question whether the methodology has been hollowed out by consultancy. Service design extends the framework to hospitals and government.
now.open_questions: How can user-centred methods reach groups not represented in original research?

items.reflection: Design thinking taught non-designers that empathy is a tool.

moments.title: Velcro invented
moments.body: De Mestral notices burrs sticking to his dog's fur after a walk and turns the observation into a patented hook-and-loop fastener (1955).
moments.takeaway: Biomimicry can start with a walk in the woods.

moments.title: Eastgate Centre
moments.body: Pearce designs an office building whose passive cooling mimics termite mounds, drastically reducing air-conditioning needs.
moments.takeaway: Buildings can borrow from biology to save energy.

moments.title: Biomimicry book
moments.body: Benyus's 'Biomimicry: Innovation Inspired by Nature' names a movement and field.
moments.takeaway: Books can crystallise scattered practices into named disciplines.

now.title: Biomimicry now
now.body: AskNature.org catalogues biological strategies for designers. Engineering courses include biomimicry as standard.
now.open_questions: Can biomimicry compete with brute-force engineering on cost?

items.reflection: Nature has had longer to debug its designs than any human engineer.

moments.title: Term 'universal design' coined
moments.body: Mace, a polio survivor and architect, introduces 'universal design' as design usable by all without adaptation.
moments.takeaway: Disability advocates have shaped mainstream design vocabulary.

moments.title: Seven principles published
moments.body: The Center for Universal Design articulates seven principles, from equitable use to size and space for approach.
moments.takeaway: Frameworks help designers translate values into checklists.

moments.title: UN Convention on Rights of Persons with Disabilities
moments.body: The convention includes universal design in its definitions, embedding the concept in international law.
moments.takeaway: Design philosophy can become legal commitment.

now.title: Inclusive design today
now.body: Microsoft's Inclusive Design Toolkit (2016) extends thinking beyond disability to situational and temporary needs.
now.open_questions: What does universal design look like for AI products?

items.reflection: Curb cuts were demanded by disabled veterans; everyone uses them now.

moments.title: Wegner's Round Chair
moments.body: Wegner's chair is featured by Interiors magazine as 'the most beautiful chair in the world'. The Nixon-Kennedy debate (1960) uses copies.
moments.takeaway: Magazines made Scandinavian design a global aesthetic.

moments.title: Alvar Aalto's Paimio chair
moments.body: Aalto designs a bent-plywood lounge chair for tuberculosis patients, embodying humane modernism.
moments.takeaway: Medical contexts have driven major furniture design.

moments.title: Egg chair
moments.body: Jacobsen designs the Egg for the SAS Royal Hotel, a single-piece sculptural lounge chair.
moments.takeaway: Hotels patronised some of modernism's most iconic furniture.

now.title: Scandinavian design now
now.body: Hygge marketing, IKEA's global reach and Nordic design ethics shape global furniture aesthetics.
now.open_questions: How do mass-market and luxury Scandinavian design coexist?

items.reflection: Curved wood, sparse rooms and natural light became a 20th-century global ideal.

moments.title: Model T launched
moments.body: The Model T is offered at $825 in 1908 and falls to $260 by 1925, accessible to working families.
moments.takeaway: Manufacturing engineering can shape demographic patterns.

moments.title: Moving assembly line
moments.body: Ford reduces Model T assembly from 12 hours to 90 minutes by introducing a moving line.
moments.takeaway: Process redesign can outdo product redesign.

moments.title: Tesla Roadster
moments.body: Tesla launches its first production electric car, beginning a re-engineering of the automobile.
moments.takeaway: Established industries can be reset by single product launches.

now.title: Cars today
now.body: EV adoption, autonomous driving and shared mobility reshape an industry built around private ownership.
now.open_questions: Will cars look anything like cars in 30 years?

items.reflection: The Model T's century has ended; what replaces it is being designed now.

moments.title: Tetra Pak filed
moments.body: The original tetrahedral milk carton enters production, with later rectangular cartons revolutionising ambient milk distribution.
moments.takeaway: Packaging design is itself a major industrial design field.

moments.title: First UPC scanned
moments.body: A 10-pack of Wrigley's gum is the first product scanned by Universal Product Code (barcode).
moments.takeaway: Retail logistics depend on graphical conventions.

moments.title: Plastic packaging targets
moments.body: The EU adopts the Single-Use Plastics Directive; the UK introduces a Plastic Packaging Tax in 2022.
moments.takeaway: Regulation reshapes what packaging is allowed.

now.title: Packaging today
now.body: Refill stations, edible packaging and reusable systems compete with single-use plastic. Design briefs increasingly include end-of-life routes.
now.open_questions: Can packaging be redesigned out of existence for many product categories?

items.reflection: Most people see more designed packaging in a day than designed objects.

moments.title: Xerox Star launched
moments.body: The first commercial GUI machine with windows, icons and a mouse, the Star is too expensive but seeds Apple and Microsoft's interfaces.
moments.takeaway: Research labs design futures that other companies sell.

moments.title: iPhone touch interface
moments.body: Multi-touch becomes the default interaction model for personal computing.
moments.takeaway: Hardware design reshaped what software design had to be.

moments.title: ChatGPT released
moments.body: Conversational AI becomes a public product, raising new questions about interface design.
moments.takeaway: Designing for conversation differs from designing for screens.

now.title: UX today
now.body: AI, voice and AR push interaction design into new territory. Dark patterns and addictive design face regulatory attention.
now.open_questions: What will replace 'apps' as the dominant interface metaphor?

items.reflection: Most product design today is interaction design.

moments.title: Zara's rapid model
moments.body: Zara compresses design-to-shelf cycles to 2-3 weeks, popularising fast fashion.
moments.takeaway: Manufacturing speed became a design strategy.

moments.title: Rana Plaza collapse
moments.body: 1,134 garment workers die in a building collapse, prompting the Accord on Fire and Building Safety.
moments.takeaway: Cheap clothing's hidden costs became globally visible.

moments.title: Shein and ultra-fast fashion
moments.body: Shein lists 6,000 new items a day, made possible by data-driven small-batch testing.
moments.takeaway: Algorithms now decide what gets manufactured.

now.title: Fashion now
now.body: EU rules on textile waste and digital product passports begin to enter force. Resale platforms grow.
now.open_questions: Can fashion be both fast and sustainable?

items.reflection: Garments are the most rapidly designed and disposed objects we make.

moments.title: Guggenheim Bilbao opens
moments.body: Gehry's titanium-clad museum is credited with reviving a post-industrial Basque city. The 'Bilbao effect' enters urban-planning vocabulary.
moments.takeaway: Single buildings can rebrand cities.

moments.title: Gehry adopts CATIA
moments.body: Gehry's team starts using aerospace software CATIA to model curved surfaces.
moments.takeaway: Cross-industry software transfers reshaped architecture.

moments.title: BIM mandates emerge
moments.body: The UK Government BIM Mandate (2011) makes Building Information Modelling required for public projects by 2016.
moments.takeaway: Computational design became a regulatory expectation.

now.title: Computational architecture
now.body: Generative design, AI-assisted layout and parametric tools shape what counts as architectural skill.
now.open_questions: What happens to craft as software writes more of the building?

items.reflection: Twentieth-century architecture's last great shift was from drawing board to algorithm.

moments.title: Crucible steel in Sheffield
moments.body: Huntsman develops a method of producing more uniform crucible steel.
moments.takeaway: Material innovations underpinned the Industrial Revolution.

moments.title: Bessemer process
moments.body: Bessemer's converter allows mass production of steel from pig iron. Steel production multiplies.
moments.takeaway: Process innovation reshapes design possibilities.

moments.title: Stainless steel
moments.body: Brearley accidentally discovers stainless steel while researching gun barrels.
moments.takeaway: Accidents have driven major materials breakthroughs.

now.title: Steel today
now.body: Green steel (hydrogen reduction) is the next industrial transition; UK steel production has declined sharply.
now.open_questions: Can steel be decarbonised at scale?

items.reflection: A single city's metallurgy shaped global manufacturing for centuries.

moments.title: Apollo program begins
moments.body: Kennedy commits the US to a moon landing within the decade. Massive design and engineering investment follows.
moments.takeaway: Political deadlines drive design innovation.

moments.title: Moon landing
moments.body: Apollo 11's guidance computer had 64KB of memory and ran on 2 MHz. The lunar module's interior is studied as a masterclass in constraint-driven design.
moments.takeaway: Hard constraints sharpen design.

moments.title: SpaceX reuse
moments.body: Rocket reuse cuts launch costs by an order of magnitude.
moments.takeaway: Design thinking about reuse changes economics.

now.title: Space design now
now.body: Commercial space puts hardware design in front of consumer audiences (Starship). Habitat design for Mars is studied seriously.
now.open_questions: How does design change in zero-G?

items.reflection: Space program design constraints continue to shape consumer technology.

moments.title: First Dyson prototype
moments.body: After 5,127 prototypes Dyson develops a bagless cyclone vacuum cleaner. He launches in Japan first as G-Force (1986).
moments.takeaway: Persistence is a design method.

moments.title: DC01 launches in UK
moments.body: Within 18 months the DC01 becomes the UK's best-selling vacuum cleaner.
moments.takeaway: Differentiated industrial design can disrupt mature markets.

moments.title: Dyson bladeless fan
moments.body: The Air Multiplier launches, applying air-amplifying technology learned from hand dryers.
moments.takeaway: Cross-product technology transfer drives novelty.

now.title: Iteration today
now.body: Rapid prototyping, simulation and consumer testing have compressed iteration cycles. Dyson's persistence approach still defines product design teaching.
now.open_questions: Can iteration alone produce category-defining products?

items.reflection: Dyson made iterative testing visible as a design philosophy.
